topics.title: EIH
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 4 - Exercise Performance/Academy - Exercise Performance 1 - EIH.txt

blocks.text: Before we get started with our discussion on Exercise Performance, we need to point out a rare but concerning phenomenon that has occurred in our high-intensity strength training circle for decades. It is what's termed an Exercise Induced Headache.

An EIH is a headache caused or associated with exertion during strength training. It is commonly described by many sufferers as starting as dull, low-intensity head pain or stiffness in the back of the head. If exercise continues, the pain can intensify and radiate over the top of the head and into the orbit of one eye. The most likely theory that exists is that it is the result of a backup of venous return causing overflow and swelling in emissary veins in the skull leading to a “pressure headache”.

It has been our experience that EIH’s rarely occur but if one does appear it is usually during one of the first few workouts or later as the subject progressively increases their intensity of effort. There also seems to be some correlation to breath holding (ValSalva) during higher levels of exertion.

Importantly, an EIH does not cause long term issues or injury and will often dissipate if the exercise is terminated immediately at the slightest sense of any head pain. For this reason, the possibility for an EIH must be introduced to all clients during the consultation as prevention is the best option.
Here are the action steps to be followed by instructors and communicated to a client as a means of prevention or in dealing with the onset of symptoms:

During the consultation, let the client know that an EIH is rare but possible. Ask the client to report any headache that they may already have prior to their session or if one develops during the workout.
SAFELY and immediately unload the weight and explain what you are feeling to your trainer.
Realize your instructor will not know what you are experiencing, so you must take the responsibility to stop the exercise.

The client  should sit on the machine or somewhere comfortable to relax. Keep the feet and legs below the heart and do not talk. Keep eyes closed and head still with head supported if needed for two minutes. Sometimes moving to a dark room can help if the client has become light sensitive. The trainer should stay with the client.

The client must be unable to even imagine the head pain for the workout to continue. If the pain does not completely vanish, terminate the workout. Several days later, attempt another workout only if the head pain is non-existent. If pain persists, consult a physician.
If you do experience an EIH there are several options within the exercise routine to help avoid them.

Drop the exercise they experienced the EIH on for several weeks. If it happened on Leg Press (most likely) do that exercise last once re-introduced. For the reintroduction of the leg press, to do so at a lowered intensity ( less weight and/or fewer reps). Remind the client to breathe freely, especially at the lower turnaround and as the intensity increases.
If an EIH occurs again, drop the exercise for the foreseeable future and take extra precaution to carefully progress client on all exercises.

Going forward then failure must be redefined in each exercise. Terminate the exercise not when concentric failure is reached, but at the very instant that the slightest head pain is sensed. Then repeat the previous steps above.
Subsequent workouts will have the new redefined failure point of imagined head pain.
It may be beneficial to start each routine with Cervical Extension to increase blood flow through the neck and upper back. It may also help to fatigue the neck musculature.

Keep accurate records to pinpoint exactly where the EIH occurs. Note whether it is consistently on the same exercise or at the same point repetition-wise. Avoid this exercise entirely as suggested above or this level of intensity by staying below this repetition count for subsequent workouts. Gradually reintroduce the exercise and/or the intensity by building back up slowly. Eventually, the entire workout should be completed without any sign of an EIH. This may take weeks of carefully tracked reintroduction but this has been a successful approach in just about every instance.

topics.title: Components of a Repetition
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 4 - Exercise Performance/Academy - Exercise Performance 2 - Components of a Repetition.txt

blocks.text: The smallest and arguably most important unit of measure of a workout is the individual repetition. Every productive workout comes down to the quality of the reps performed that make up that workout. Taking this a step further then, we can say that the long-term success of the program is largely attributable to the sum of these individual reps. For this reason, we can assign the highest level of importance to mastering the execution of the protocol. Simply stated, each subject should look to train better over time and understand that this happens on a rep to rep basis. As an aside, “training better” takes into account a multitude of factors that are explained throughout the MSF Academy and are a primary objective of the client's journey with us.
For purposes of our insight and instruction, let’s consider the following components of a repetition, which can be viewed as a cycle of five distinct phases:

The gradual load up or the handoff are the only two ways that an exercise can begin using our methodology. There is a detailed process to each of these techniques and the exercise should not begin without direction from the instructor. The client must be held accountable to properly performing the initiation of each exercise. The gradual load up along with the lower turnaround (discussed below) are quite possibly the two most critical elements of our protocol to be understood and mastered by our clients. But more importantly, this understanding and mastery has to begin with the instructor. Please review the Equipment and Instruction Scripts for the specifics [https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1f29em_iNFAcRRMwhtqW97VNOtd0Kc3wB?usp=drive_link]

The concentric (positive) phase of the movement is the lifting motion during which the target muscles contract and shorten, moving the joint(s) from the start point to the endpoint of the range of motion.

The eccentric (negative) phase of the movement is the lowering motion during which the target muscles stretch and lengthen, moving the joint(s) back from the endpoint to the start point of the range of motion.

The upper turnaround is the change of direction occurring after the concentric phase of the repetition and into the eccentric portion. It also refers to the uppermost position of the weight stack in the range of motion of an exercise.

The lower turnaround is the change of direction occurring after the eccentric portion of the repetition and into the concentric portion. It also refers to the lowermost position of the weight stack in the range of motion of an exercise.

Changes of direction, or “turnarounds”, are a critical aspect of exercise performance when it comes to safety and efficient muscular loading. This is where the potential for acceleration, and therefore increased force and momentum, is greatest. In fact, turnaround performance is more important than repetition speed alone and is the single most important attribute to master in properly performed exercise.

The lower turnaround performance for most exercises is treated with a perpetual, “touch and go” motion, where the weights being lifted would lightly touch the remaining weights not being lifted from the weight stack. The exception would be compound pulling exercises where the machine’s range of motion exceeds the involved joint’s range of motion (i.e. the elbows straighten prior to the weights touching). Most clients and even some trainers are going to underappreciate the detail, skill, and effort required to perform a proper lower turnaround, but this cannot be an afterthought. A properly performed lower turnaround (along with the gradual load up) drives proper exercise at MSF, and the Exercise Practitioner must master the technique themselves. But more importantly, they must be able to persistently teach and enforce this concept to our clients.

A proper upper turnaround varies between two different techniques depending on the type of exercise being performed. For some exercises, the subject will simply “pass-through” the upper turnaround in one continuous motion (similar to the lower turn). For other exercises, a squeeze technique, or a brief period of increasing effort in the contracted position, is performed before lowering the weight. The application of these methods is detailed more thoroughly at a later point in the manual.

As a reminder, exercises that typically have a squeeze technique are single joint movements and compound pulling exercises. Importantly, the instructor should be attentive to the need to instruct exactly HOW to squeeze on a given exercise rather than just relying on the command "squeeze." The word alone does not describe how to do it and most will likely act to clench their fists.

If we consider the leg extension, for example, we might instruct the subject to "continue to straighten the knee" or "attempt to straighten the knee further" in the contracted position (even though further movement is not possible). By attempting to straighten the knee further, the quadriceps will be forced to contract harder thus accomplishing the squeeze we are seeking. These are the details that MSF Exercise Practitioners are consistently looking to improve (Kaizen).

topics.title: Gradual Load-up
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 4 - Exercise Performance/Academy - Exercise Performance 3 - Gradual Load-up.txt

blocks.text: For all compound pushing movements and most single-joint movements, the subject begins the exercise by lifting the weight from a dead stop in the stretched position. It is critical that the initial application of force, or load-up, be performed with the most attentive focus on being gradual or incremental with the pressure applied.

Most trainees produce a sudden exertion while simultaneously holding their breath (Valsalva) in order to get the movement started most efficiently. This is an instinctive measure taken by the body as it is in a biomechanically disadvantaged position. Clients will often exclaim, "I needed to make sure I could lift it."  Or sometimes the opposite will happen where a subject will push abruptly and then instantly stop if the load doesn't move immediately. At this point, they'll tell their trainer that they "can't lift the weight."

In either case, they have already forgotten the REAL OBJECTIVE of resistance training that was taught during the consultation; to create mechanical tension in as many muscle fibers (motor unit recruitment) of the targeted musculature as possible. It is imperative for the trainer to remind or re-teach the client how to properly initiate an exercise that begins from an unloaded, dead stop.

Assuming the selected weight is appropriate, and the client is properly positioned and braced, there needs to be a GRADUAL application of force concurrent with a continuous and free breathing pattern. The subject needs to "go through their gears," so to speak, in an attempt to find the minimum level of force required to actually begin lifting the load. This should take several seconds or longer, depending on the magnitude of the load. Reassure them that it is in their best interest to take the challenge of proper resistance training seriously, and the load-up, in particular, to make the exercise significantly safer and more effective.

By attempting to master the GRADUAL LOAD-UP, the trainee will be able to get a better effect by creating more tension with less weight, thus reducing risk. They should also strive to make this gradual load-up a priority so as to control another variable in the progressive overload of exercise. If one were to suddenly apply force while holding their breath, they would more easily lift the weight, which may cause the trainer to believe a load increase is warranted. This would be premature, however, and would likely lead to deteriorating form and lack of control of the movement and could expose the client to excessive loading.

To illustrate this gradual load-up, let us consider the leg extension. Note that the first 15-30 degrees in the leg extension movement occurs almost at once if not closely controlled. Meaningful tension is then obviated by the momentum employed to begin the exercise. If not properly instructed and enforced by the trainer, this habit will only worsen over time, leading to ineffective and potentially dangerous exercise. Instead, consider the following mental imagery to help learn how to properly apply a gradual effort:

Sit on the leg extension machine in the start position. Suppose that the load on the machine is set to 100lbs. With no intention to move right away, start to slightly push the shins into the tibia pad thus engaging the quadriceps muscles. Try and produce a minimal effort of only 10 lbs and note that as expected, there is no movement.

Now gradually begin to increase the force to 20 lbs; then 30; then 40; then 50. At this point, you might notice the tibia pads begin to compress from the applied pressure. Continue to increase the force to 60 lbs; then 70; then 80; then 90; then 100. Still, no movement occurs and again this is all by design and needs to be expected.

Then apply 101 lbs of force. After the tibia pad fully compresses, the belts/cables tighten, the body sinks into the seat and slightly contorts, the movement arm flexes and when just enough force is applied, the movement arm (and load) will begin to move. In other words, all of the slack in the system, both in the machine and the body, must be taken out through tightening or compressing before movement can occur. This is the level of detail that the subject needs to understand and practice to properly learn the gradual load up.

This entire mental picture is applied over a time frame of 3 or more seconds. For exercises with larger loads, like a leg press, a properly performed load-up may take 5 seconds or more. Regardless of the actual time taken, the concept is the same; a gradual buildup of force resulting in a gradual introduction of mechanical tension to the targeted muscles. The Exercise Practitioner must make every effort to reinforce this critical concept of the MSF Continuous Tension protocol to ensure the safety and improve the effectiveness of our client's experience.

topics.title: Range of Motion
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 4 - Exercise Performance/Academy - Exercise Performance 4 - Range of Motion.txt

blocks.text: Exercises are performed through the safest and most effective range of motion for each individual on every movement. The range of motion used is specific to the client and the exercise and should be constantly evaluated by the instructor; even for advanced clients that may have used a particular piece of equipment dozens of times. Exercise Practitioners are always looking for ways to optimize the clients' experience.

Safe range of motion refers to the distance over which the involved muscles and joints are not exposed to potentially harmful forces, or the range over which an individual does not experience pain due to an existing injury or physical condition. For example, the start position (and lower turnaround) on the seated leg curl is set to avoid hyperextending the knee.

If a client's tolerable range of motion on an exercise is limited due to injury, pain, or lack of flexibility, the range of motion of the machine should be adjusted to accommodate this. This should be clearly indicated on the client's chart along with all other settings and updated for any changes over time. Keep in mind that as a trainee gains strength on an exercise where they were previously limited, the range of motion may be increased as a form of progression.

Effective range of motion refers to the range over which the target muscles encounter meaningful and balanced resistance. For example, the targeted muscles of the frontal thighs encounter little resistance as the knee approaches the extended position on the leg press. In fact, it is likely that the muscles actually unload and rest to some extent with the load being supported by the bones. As a result, excessive knee extension should be avoided on the leg press as it falls outside of the effective range. Compare that to a leg extension where the quadriceps are in their most contracted position as the knee straightens. In this case, we want to take advantage of this by having the subject straighten the knee as fully as possible to create more meaningful tension.

The range of motion used may need to be adjusted at any moment for any client, given any number of variables discussed throughout the manual. The instructor should be proactively attentive to creating the most optimal experience for every client on every exercise of every workout. This is another element of the Exercise Practitioner's expertise that needs to be mastered as they continue to develop their craft.

topics.title: Speed of Movement
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 4 - Exercise Performance/Academy - Exercise Performance 5 - Speed of Movement.txt

blocks.text: Repetitions are performed slowly enough to allow for a smooth reversal of direction between the positive and negative phases of movement (turnaround technique) while allowing the trainee to maintain proper posture, positioning and/or alignment throughout the exercise. Reversing direction smoothly prevents potentially harmful increases in force that can result from sudden movement and helps maintain continuous tension on the targeted muscles. It also protects against the all too common tendency to instinctively unload and then abruptly load back up again in an effort to escape the mounting discomfort. This is one of the more dangerous discrepancies as there tends to be a lack of awareness while this sudden act is happening.

An approximate 12 to 20-second repetition cycle, consisting of a 6 to 10-second positive, followed by a brief pause in the contracted position or continuous upper turnaround,  and then a 6 to 10-second negative, followed by a continuous lower turnaround, appears to be adequately slow for this purpose. A slower repetition cycle is beneficial when instructing novice trainees or when working with trainees with injuries or conditions requiring extra caution.

When introducing a client to the protocol or a new exercise, a verbal cadence count can be used to assist the client in experiencing the feel of a properly controlled movement. Using an occasional cadence for experienced clients if they begin to move too slowly or too quickly can also be helpful.

A shorter (closer to 6) or longer (closer to 10) cadence count is acceptable for exercises with shorter or longer ranges of motion, respectively; however, to avoid confusing the client, it is best to use a consistent repetition cadence whenever possible. And more importantly, the speed of movement should be the same on both the concentric and eccentric phases of a repetition. Importantly, while subjects are encouraged to maintain their pace, one cannot and should not expect their EFFORT to remain constant. In other words, if we are to maintain a given pace in an activity with increasing fatigue, our effort needs to voluntarily increase to counter that fatigue. This is how stimulative mechanical tension is created. This is what makes resistance training effective.

In this way, pace governs effort. As the subject senses their movement bogging down, they should be encouraged to push harder to maintain the pace. There’s a point in the set where the subject is no longer moving slowly because they’re supposed to move slowly (voluntarily). They’re moving slowly because they are beginning to fatigue and could not speed up (involuntarily).

It’s not enough to move slowly until we can no longer move at the selected pace or because we can no longer tolerate the discomfort. It is critical to recognize this and to provide the proper encouragement and teaching points as we help our clients cultivate this ability to train harder. And while we’re on the topic of discomfort, by focusing instead on one’s pace, it may help to get beyond the adverse feelings that often lead to the premature ending of sets.

Also of note, as a client becomes more advanced, it will likely be in their best interest to move closer to the 6-second pace. A faster pace will be easier to control and will afford a smoother repetition (with practice). It will also create less discomfort which as we know will allow for a higher level of effort. As mentioned, this will take practice and may take months to fully implement.

It cannot be said enough, that this faster pace may NOT be for every client. Only those that show an understanding, a tolerance, and an above average competency to maintain their quality while training at this higher intensity. There will still be situations where a slower, closer to 10-second pace will be optimal and a faster pace should never be forced. At the end of the day, the safety of each individual client is our main priority.

topics.title: Turnaround Technique
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 4 - Exercise Performance/Academy - Exercise Performance 6 - Turnaround Technique.txt

blocks.text: Proper turnaround performance varies depending on the characteristics of the start and endpoints of an exercise and whether mechanical or anatomical structures or leverage factors limit the range of motion. Turnaround performance should prevent the unloading of target muscles and avoid placing the involved joints or muscular structures in potentially harmful positions.

When the equipment used allows the resistance source to be set down and unloaded at the start point, such as the weights being lifted touching the weights not being lifted on a selectorized machine, the trainee should:

Reduce speed as the weight approaches the start point (lower turnaround) during the negative enough to ensure a minimized impact. Ultimately we are looking for exaggerated control in the most challenging part of the movement.
Allow the weights lifted to touch the remaining weights in the stack without being set down or unloading the target musculature. This ensures a consistent and full range of motion.
Immediately but slowly begin the positive phase of the movement. This is commonly instructed as “barely touch, barely start,” “touch and go,” or "be continuous."

This is the situation that would occur for all compound pushing movements (e.g. leg press, chest press, overhead press) and most single-joint or rotary exercises (e.g. leg extension, leg curl, lateral raise).
When the range of motion of the equipment used exceeds the trainee’s range of motion and the negative movement is limited by the involved joint structures, the trainee should:
Reduce speed as the involved joint approaches the position of the lower turnaround. This helps prevent the joint from being forced beyond its tolerable range of motion.
Immediately but slowly begin the positive phase of the movement.

In a compound row or a pulldown, for example, the elbow joint would most likely straighten completely before the weights being lifted bottomed out. This would define the lower turnaround, and the change of direction would happen as the elbow joint straightened.
When the range of motion of the equipment used exceeds the trainee’s range of motion and the negative movement is limited by the flexibility of the involved muscular structures, the trainee should:
Reduce speed as the weight approaches the start point (lower turnaround).
Carefully enter into an abbreviated, moderate stretch.
Immediately but slowly begin the positive phase of the movement.

An example of this might be a valgus elbow that doesn’t allow for complete straightening at the lower turn. In this case, the subject would extend the elbow up to a point that is tolerable and then change directions. Another example would be a subject’s knee that won’t fully extend on a leg extension. In this case, a less than normal range of motion is acceptable.
When the equipment used limits positive movement, such as a leg press with a range limiter, or end stop, to prevent full knee extension, the trainee should:
Reduce speed as the movement arm approaches the end point (upper turnaround) during the positive phase of movement in order to minimize impact force.
Upon reaching the endpoint, the trainee will barely touch or “pass through” the upper turnaround (similar treatment to the lower turnaround).
Immediately but slowly begin the negative phase of the movement. Keeping the movement continuous throughout is the goal.
When performing a compound pulling movement or simple movement that provides meaningful resistance at the end of the positive range of motion (i.e. contracted position), the trainee should:
Reduce speed as the movement arm approaches the finished position to minimize momentum.
Pause definitely and briefly (one or two seconds) in the finished position. This is known as the contracted position.
Gradually ease out of the contracted position.
Slowly begin the negative.

After a continuous lower turnaround and starting with the third repetition, the trainee focuses on intensely contracting the target muscles by keeping the movement arm and body completely still. This is known as the "squeeze technique" and is employed from the third rep on and should generally last for 2 to 3 seconds before easing out. This is simply another way to create mechanical tension in the targeted musculature.
If the range of motion of the involved joints or muscular structures exceeds the range over which the target muscles are meaningfully loaded, the trainee should:

Begin the turnaround as soon as the load noticeably begins to decrease to avoid unloading. Examples of this would include changing direction before the shoulders are unloaded at the lower turnaround of a dumbbell lateral raise and turning around before full extension during compound pushing movements, as in a bodyweight squat. Some abdominal machines can be moved with the limbs beyond the point of a fully contracted abdomen, but this situation will almost never occur on properly designed selectorized machines. The Exercise Practitioner must be aware of this and ensure that the movements are performed in the most optimal range.

In all cases described above, there is one common attribute; a smooth and continuous lower turnaround. And in most cases, the upper turnaround should be smooth and continuous as well. This may very well be THE most important concept in the execution of the MSF Continuous Tension method.

topics.title: Set Duration
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 4 - Exercise Performance/Academy - Exercise Performance 7 - Set Duration.txt

blocks.text: Typically, we aim to perform somewhere between 6 to 10 repetitions before reaching concentric failure in a set of exercise. When learning a new exercise, the expected set duration will likely be a little longer than in most other situations. Anywhere from 8 to 15 repetitions may be more optimal in this case. Lighter weight and higher repetitions lend themselves to a more meaningful learning experience for the client. It provides an opportunity to focus more easily on the details of the protocol, to take direction, and to exhibit the exaggerated control of movement we are seeking. As the client becomes more proficient at performing the exercise, the load will likely be increased, but not every workout and not indefinitely. It’s also the last variable of progressive overload that should be increased, as will be discussed later.

For the majority of intermediate and advanced level subjects, set durations where the trainee is unable to complete at least five reps is an indication that the weight may be too heavy. For the upper limit, the intermediate or advanced subject should be expected to reach muscular failure (or as close as is tolerable) within 10 repetitions at the most, otherwise the load may be too light. Importantly, these parameters are not set in stone but rather guidance put in place to facilitate load selection. We want each exercise to be challenging but still well within the client’s control.

Clients who may respond better to shorter set durations may have difficulty continuing an exercise beyond a particular number of reps. This may be due to the predominance of a muscle fiber type, psychological factors, or afferent feedback from the working muscles (i.e. extreme discomfort or 'burning"). These are just some of the reasons higher repetition sets can be considered less than optimal.

Some clients may benefit from longer set durations. For them, their form may begin to deteriorate if the resistance level is progressed too quickly and their set duration is reduced below a certain point. Or, in keeping with the above, this could also be due to fiber makeup or psychological profile. There are a good number of people that simply don't like the feeling of physical exertion, and a perceived "heavy" weight will exacerbate this. These clients need to be instructed and progressed differently than those that thrive with a physical challenge. But in most of these cases, the intensity adverse subjects can learn to tolerate and even fully accept the demands of resistance training. This is an attribute of exercise progression that one should attempt to improve on every rep of every exercise of every workout. This may also be the most challenging aspect of resistance training to teach and master; to overcome the aversion to intense muscular effort.

Again, repetitions should always be performed continuously, with every effort made to avoid unloading the target muscles. Repetitions are performed until the client is unable to continue positive movement with proper form, thus achieving full motor unit recruitment and meaningful mechanical tension.

topics.title: Rest Interval Between Exercises
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 4 - Exercise Performance/Academy - Exercise Performance 8 - Rest Interval Between Exercises.txt

blocks.text: A common belief and practice in the high-intensity realm is that workouts should be conducted with as little rest or downtime as possible in between exercises. The intent behind this strategy is multifaceted. The primary reasoning is based on the faulty belief that fatigue is a necessary component in creating a hypertrophy stimulus. Basically, if one were to rush through a workout, they would create more fatigue, resulting in a stronger stimulus. But fatigue is not a stimulus for hypertrophy, in fact it is a hindrance that will diminish the effect of the workout as is explained below.

Another reason HIT practitioners have recommended maintaining a brisk pace throughout the workout is for purposes of safety. The theory is that by never fully recovering from one exercise to the other, the subject will be challenged with less weight. And on the surface, a lighter load is probably safer. But let’s consider the following logic. Firstly, we need to remember that the service we provide at MSF is dedicated strength training. Because of this, we must approach our workouts in a manner that optimizes the physiology of stimulating strength and hypertrophy. We do not want to turn our workouts into cardio sessions. This means challenging the body up to and beyond its current strength capabilities. Well, anything that reduces our output during a workout will result in an effort that is below the body’s current capabilities, which will not be stimulative toward strength or hypertrophy.

The net effect of training in a fatigued state is that our motor unit recruitment (MUR) will be greatly diminished. Importantly, as a protective mechanism, our nervous system will not sustain a high level of effort in an increasingly fatigued state. It governs this by limiting the signal sent from the Central Motor Command of the brain, which activates our motor units (i.e. muscle fibers). This is not a matter of will, it is a matter of physiology. Yes, with consistent training we can become more fatigue resistant, but in the moment, we must do what is necessary to maximize our current capacity to recruit motor units. Remember, if a motor unit is not first activated, its muscle fibers cannot be stimulated.

With this in mind, it makes sense to allow for some recovery between sets of exercise. “Recovery” in this case will most likely be cardiorespiratory. Essentially we should allow the clients to at least begin to catch their breath. While they may not fully return to resting levels because of time and deconditioning, it should still begin to normalize after 60 - 120 seconds or so. The extent to which their breathing does not fully normalize will be the fatigue resistance or “cardio” benefit that is stimulated to improve over time. Keep in mind, this will not be something that we will time necessarily, but rather use observation and good judgement. The main point here is just to make sure that we do not rush between movements. We should seek the highest level of output from each individual exercise, while recognizing that fatigue is not entirely avoidable.

One last consideration on the topic of intra-workout recovery would be the specific exercises selected and the sequence we choose to run them in. If we are performing larger compound movements (think Big 5) and put them back to back to back, it is going to create substantially more oxygen debt. We would want to allow for more time between these movements than we would if we put a biceps curl after adduction for example. So keep this in mind along with watching for feedback while instructing a workout. Also, movements that affect one another directly, like in a designed prefatigue, will absolutely reduce performance of the second in the pairing (e.g. chest flye into chest press). That is not to say we would never use a prefatigue, but it would have to be used selectively and for the right reasons. Otherwise, splitting up the overlapping exercises would result in a higher level of effort, which results in a more profound stimulus. It may also be the difference between creating a stimulus and not creating one. So program the workouts intelligently and watch closely to how they play out on the studio floor. Make adjustments based on the findings and discuss them with your team. Kaizen!

topics.title: Number of Sets
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 4 - Exercise Performance/Academy - Exercise Performance 9 - Number of Sets.txt

blocks.text: In most cases, only one set is performed per exercise. The majority of research shows no significant benefit for most people to perform more than one set of an exercise as long as that set is taken to or close to muscular failure. This is the best way to ensure that the stimulus created from the exercise is recoverable and emphasizes the ideal that the quality of the effort is paramount. If one is to perform only a single set of an exercise, one must utilize every bit of focus and intensity that can be called upon.

Exceptions to this may include certain rehab situations or for severely deconditioned or extremely intensity adverse clients. In these cases, multiple sets performed at a sub-maximal level of effort may be beneficial. In rare cases, a rest-pause may be used for more experienced trainees that may have just “mistimed” their effort. Importantly, it is the responsibility of the MSF Exercise Practitioner to ensure a productive workout for the client. In the event that an experienced client is just having an “off day” or has just lost focus for a moment and prematurely ended their set, a second attempt may be performed. This second attempt should be employed only after a sufficient rest period where the client is able to catch their breath and consideration should be given to reducing the weight. It is also imperative that this approach does not become a regular occurrence or used as a crutch in place of proper focus and technique. But in rare situations, it may help to ensure the client is satisfied with their effort and the workout.

topics.title: Warm-up Considerations
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 4 - Exercise Performance/Academy - Exercise Performance 10 - Warm-up Considerations.txt

blocks.text: For general exercise, a separate warm-up set is unnecessary. Assuming an appropriate level of resistance, the first several repetitions provide all the warm-up necessary for the exercise.

By initially fatiguing the target musculature we prepare it to safely perform maximum effort later in the same set. A muscle is less likely to be able to injure itself in a fatigued state as its force capability is greatly diminished well below the tensile strength of the tendons and ligaments. Again, this assumes proper behavior and execution during the entire exercise.

Also, consider that the mechanical action of the exercise allows for the membranous fluids to flow more freely and lubricate the muscles and joints. For these reasons, the most direct and efficient approach to warm-up is performing the exercise itself. Of course, the exception to this would be a subject with a joint debility where a lighter exercise to work the joint might be performed prior to a more challenging effort (e.g. leg curl preceding a leg press for a knee replacement recipient).
